title: Flash sale at 2.5x: the pool that wasn't big enough

author.name: Sample senior SRE
author.note: Example mod written for the MVP

story: You are on call for the checkout API. Marketing is running a surprise flash sale this morning; nobody told the platform team the expected traffic. The API runs 4 pods behind an edge proxy, with a read-through cache in front of Postgres (max 100 connections, each pod holds a pool of 20). Watch the dashboard, decide, act. Changes take time to land, just like in prod.

timeline.message: Heads up, the flash sale banner goes live in a couple of minutes!

timeline.deploy: marketing: homepage banner + 400 new SKUs published

timeline.message: Disk 86% on logs-02. Is that related?
Customers on Twitter say checkout is spinning. What's the ETA?
Sale traffic is holding steady, it should stay like this for the rest of the hour.

runbook.title: Stop the bleeding before you understand it
runbook.detail: Errors are burning the budget every second. Shed load at the edge first: a clean 429 for some users beats timeouts for all of them.

runbook.title: Find the actual bottleneck
runbook.detail: CPU high? DB connections at the limit? Look at both. The tier that is saturated is the one to fix, not the one that alerted first.

runbook.title: Check what retries are doing
runbook.detail: If offered load is higher than real user traffic, clients are retrying into a full system. That turns a slowdown into an outage.

runbook.title: Before scaling pods, do the connection math
runbook.detail: pods x pool_size must stay under the DB's max_connections. More pods can mean fewer working connections.

runbook.title: Fix the cause, then lift the limit
runbook.detail: Cold cache after a big catalog publish is common. Warm it, then raise or remove the rate limit and watch.

runbook.title: Say something
runbook.detail: Declare the incident and post an update before anyone has to ask.

expert_path.why: Name it early. It gets you help and stops side conversations.
Bought time within a minute. Users got fast 429s instead of 3s timeouts.
Offered load was ~1.6x real traffic. Retries were the second wave.
One sentence to stakeholders: impact, what we're doing, next update time.
The real cause: 400 new SKUs meant a cold cache, so 4x more DB queries per request.
Only needed if you scale pods. Keep pods x pool under max_connections.
Once the cache is warm, let the traffic back in and watch the error rate.

pitfalls.text: Scaling the API is the reflex. Here it added connections the DB didn't have: 6 pods x 20 > 100, so the DB thrashed and got slower. If you scaled, did you right-size the pool too?
A restart drops half your capacity at the worst moment. Nothing was wrong with the pods themselves.

lessons: Saturation shows up in the cheapest-to-measure place first (CPU), not always where it starts (DB connections).
Retries are load. A system at 100% with naive retries settles at an error rate far worse than the overload alone.
The disk alert on logs-02 was noise. Real incidents always have one.
debrief.senior_note: The first time this happened to me I scaled the API from 4 to 12 pods and took Postgres down with connection churn. The fix that actually worked was boring: shed load, warm the cache, then slowly let traffic back.
